title: I've been making games manually for years. Now I'm experimenting with AI and vibe coding. Here's what I learned.
author: Beneficial_Map9355
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I've been developing games manually for many years, but recently I decided to experiment with a completely different approach: AI-assisted development and vibe coding.

The result is **Pitchfork Math**, a humorous tactical survival strategy game about leading groups of peasants into ridiculous battles.

The idea started with market research. I was looking for a gap in the Steam market, something that could combine an unusual concept, humor and engaging gameplay. After identifying an opportunity, I started managing the project and gradually building a production workflow around AI tools.

# My AI development workflow

* **Claude:** My main development partner. I use it for vibe coding, programming, project management, problem-solving and coordinating the implementation of new technologies.
* **Higgsfield:** Part of my visual and video production workflow.
* **ElevenLabs:** Used to generate sound and audio assets.
* **Remotion:** I introduced it into the workflow for video production. Claude generated the code needed to create videos programmatically.

What's interesting is that I didn't start with a complete AI production pipeline. I started with an idea and gradually introduced new tools and technologies as the project evolved.

# What turned out to be the hardest part?

Honestly, manual testing.

AI can generate features and implement systems surprisingly quickly, but that doesn't mean the result is immediately playable or polished.

I spent a lot of time testing the game, finding bugs and going back and forth with Claude to fix things it had overlooked.

This included:

* Fixing UI problems and improving the overall interface.
* Finding and correcting audio issues.
* Adjusting gameplay mechanics and balancing encounters.
* Identifying missing features and edge cases that AI simply hadn't considered.
* Reworking systems that looked correct in code but didn't feel right during actual gameplay.

There were also moments when Claude suggested that we had done enough. Meanwhile, I was already thinking about adding more biomes, mechanics and content.

I quickly learned that knowing what to ask for, noticing what is missing and knowing when something simply doesn't feel right are still extremely important skills.

# The unexpected part: players became part of the development process

One of the most valuable sources of ideas turned out to be people following my social media accounts.

They watch gameplay clips, share their thoughts and suggest things they would like to see in the game. Some of these suggestions have inspired new features and additions.

In a way, the community has become another part of my development feedback loop. AI helps me implement ideas, but players often help me discover which ideas are worth implementing in the first place.

# I'd love to hear your thoughts

I've spent years developing games the traditional way, and now I'm trying to understand what this new workflow really changes.

* Have you used vibe coding to build a complete game rather than just a prototype?
* Do you also find manual testing and iteration to be the biggest bottleneck?
* How do you deal with features that AI considers finished but that still need significant work?
* Do you involve your community in deciding what to develop next?
* Where do you think the biggest limitations of AI-assisted game development currently are?

I'm genuinely interested in both positive and critical experiences, especially from developers who have worked with traditional workflows and AI-assisted development.

If you'd like to see what came out of this experiment, I've included a gameplay video.
